\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{しま} (shima)}{しま (shima)}]{\ja{しま} (shima) — an island}

\label{lesson:JA-C44-shima}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a cloud; a spider, then the Japanese for the sun.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{しま}}
\textbf{\ja{しま}} — \emph{shima} — \textquotedblleft{}an island\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{しま}} (\emph{shima}) is a native Japanese word, inherited rather than borrowed from Chinese, and its older origin is not settled. Its kanji was attached to it later as a kun'yomi, a native reading given to a Chinese character (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{shima}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{shima}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{shima}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Japanese for a cloud; a spider, then the Japanese for the sun, then say \emph{shima} again
\end{itemize}

\label{lesson:JA-C44-ame}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for soil, then the Japanese for a seed.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{あめ}}
\textbf{\ja{あめ}} — \emph{ame} — \textquotedblleft{}rain; candy\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{あめ}} (\emph{ame}) is two native words that sound alike: \emph{ame}, \textquotedblleft{}rain\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{ame}, \textquotedblleft{}candy\textquotedblright{}, each with its own kanji (JMdict). Both are inherited rather than borrowed, and are told apart by their pitch.
\end{cousinweb}
